lessons.objective: Stop a worker cooperatively when its caller no longer needs the result.
lessons.title: Stop a worker when its caller leaves
lessons.explanation: A Go context signals that work is no longer needed; it does not terminate a goroutine. The caller owns the cancel function and should invoke it when it no longer needs the result. A worker must observe ctx.Done() at blocking or repeated work boundaries and return promptly. Pass the context into downstream calls that support it; do not replace it with context.Background() inside the worker. A deadline bounds waiting, but cleanup still belongs to the worker. Assume the standard library context API.
lessons.workedExample: A search handler starts a worker to read batches from an index. The handler creates ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second), defers cancel(), and passes ctx to the worker. In its loop the worker selects between ctx.Done() (return ctx.Err()) and the next batch signal. If the client disconnects, r.Context() is canceled; the derived context signals the worker even before the two-second timeout. The worker closes only resources it owns, not ctx.Done().
lessons.exercise: A handler launches a goroutine that waits on a results channel before replying. The client can disconnect while the goroutine is waiting; no one then reads its result. Describe a cancellation-aware send and who calls cancel. What should the worker do after observing cancellation?
lessons.referenceAnswer: Derive ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(r.Context()) in the handler and defer cancel(). The worker should select { case results <- value: case <-ctx.Done(): return } rather than send unconditionally. Pass ctx to any cancellable fetch and check its error. When the handler returns or the request is canceled, the worker releases its own resources and exits; cancel only signals, it does not join the goroutine.
selfCheckCriteria: Names the handler as owner of cancel and calls it on exit.
Makes the channel send selectable against ctx.Done() so it cannot wait forever.
Explains that cancellation is cooperative and the worker must return and clean up.
lessons.provenance: Original Kontrol starter lesson; docs/learning-curriculum.md: Go / Context cancellation; Go standard library context package semantics

lessons.objective: Express independent normal, boundary, and failure cases as a table with precise expected outcomes.
lessons.title: Design table-driven tests for boundary cases
lessons.explanation: In Go 1.22+, a table of named inputs and expected outputs keeps related cases visible without duplicating test setup. Iterate over the table and use t.Run to report a distinct subtest for each case. Compare the actual result with the expected result and report both, rather than only checking that an error occurred. Include a zero or empty input and an invalid input alongside the happy path. Do not share mutable fixtures between cases; subtests may eventually run in parallel. With Go 1.22 loop variables are per iteration, but use explicit captures if supporting older Go releases.
lessons.workedExample: For a ParsePort(string) (int, error) function, cases named valid, zero, too-large, and not-a-number specify inputs "8080", "0", "65536", and "oops". The valid case expects 8080 and no error; the others expect an error. t.Run(tc.name, ...) reports which input failed. A separate test verifies whether surrounding whitespace is accepted, rather than assuming behavior not promised by the parser contract.
lessons.exercise: Write a Go test for a function clamp(n, lo, hi int) int, assuming lo <= hi. Cover n below lo, at lo, inside, at hi, and above hi; name each case. Show the loop, subtest, and failure message. What additional test would you add if lo > hi is part of the function contract?
lessons.referenceAnswer: func TestClamp(t *testing.T) { cases := []struct { name string; n, lo, hi, want int }{{"below", -2, 0, 10, 0}, {"lower", 0, 0, 10, 0}, {"inside", 6, 0, 10, 6}, {"upper", 10, 0, 10, 10}, {"above", 12, 0, 10, 10}}; for _, tc := range cases { t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) { if got := clamp(tc.n, tc.lo, tc.hi); got != tc.want { t.Errorf("clamp(%d,%d,%d) = %d, want %d", tc.n, tc.lo, tc.hi, got, tc.want) } }) } }. If inverted bounds are supported, add an explicit inverted-bounds case with an expected result defined by the API; do not guess its behavior.
selfCheckCriteria: Names all five boundary partitions and their expected values.
Uses t.Run and reports got and want for the failing case.
Does not claim behavior for inverted bounds without a contract.
lessons.provenance: Go 1.22+; reviewed against Go testing package (pkg.go.dev/testing), subtests and loopvar change (go.dev/blog/subtests; go.dev/blog/loopvar-preview); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Design a consumer-owned Go interface containing only the methods needed by that consumer.
lessons.title: Specify the small contract at the consumer
lessons.explanation: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly by a type that implements their method set. A consumer can declare the minimal behavior it needs without requiring every producer to depend on a shared broad interface. This supports substitution in tests and reduces accidental coupling. Return a concrete type from a constructor unless callers genuinely need an abstraction. An interface with one method is not automatically better: when the consumer has only one implementation and no boundary to replace, a concrete parameter may be clearer. Assume Go 1.22 standard library interfaces and method-set rules.
lessons.workedExample: A report renderer needs to send its output, not administer a whole mail service. It declares type Sender interface { Send(context.Context, []byte) error } and accepts a Sender in RenderAndSend. A production SMTP adapter and a recording test sender each implement Send; neither needs a no-op DeleteMailbox method. The handler checks and returns send errors, while the caller owns adapter lifetime.
lessons.exercise: Design the dependency boundary for a handler that must fetch a customer by ID, then format a receipt. The existing Storage type also has DeleteAll and Migrate. Specify the smallest interface, where to declare it, and how to test a missing customer and a storage failure. State when you would instead pass a concrete storage value.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Declare type CustomerFinder interface { FindCustomer(ctx context.Context, id string) (Customer, error) } beside the handler that consumes it. Accept CustomerFinder in the handler; the existing storage implements the method without importing the consumer package. Use a stub returning a not-found error to check the handler response and a second stub returning an unexpected failure to check error propagation. Do not add DeleteAll or Migrate. If the handler has no alternative implementation or test seam, accepting the concrete storage type is also reasonable; abstract at an actual boundary.
selfCheckCriteria: Keeps only FindCustomer in the consumer contract, without destructive storage methods.
Locates the interface near the consumer and exercises two distinct error cases.
Explains when a concrete dependency is simpler and does not invent an explicit implements declaration.
lessons.provenance: Go 1.22+; reviewed against Go language specification Interface types and Method sets (go.dev/ref/spec#Interface_types; go.dev/ref/spec#Method_sets), Go Code Review Comments Interfaces (go.dev/wiki/CodeReviewComments#interfaces); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Interpret Go benchmark comparisons using controlled work, allocation metrics, and repeated measurements.
lessons.title: Compare benchmarks without fooling yourself
lessons.explanation: Go testing benchmarks execute b.N iterations and the harness calibrates N to obtain useful timing. Run with go test -bench=. -benchmem and compare the same operation, input, environment, and compiler settings. Report ns/op and B/op or allocs/op as distinct quantities; lower allocations do not by themselves prove lower latency. Initialize expensive test data outside the timed loop and call b.ResetTimer when setup should be excluded. For noisy results, repeat runs and analyze variation rather than announcing a win from one measurement. Assume Go 1.22+ testing benchmarks.
lessons.workedExample: Two JSON encoders receive the same 10 KiB payload on the same machine. A: 42000 ns/op, 11000 B/op; B: 39000 ns/op, 18000 B/op. B appears faster in this run but allocates more bytes. If B had a cached input while A rebuilt it inside its timed loop, these numbers would not compare the same work. Re-run both with identical input preparation and repeated samples before recommending a replacement.
lessons.exercise: A report claims a new serializer is 20% faster from a single go test -bench run, but the old benchmark builds a fixture inside b.N while the new one reuses a fixture. Explain two flaws, how to restructure the benchmark loop, and which metrics and repetitions to collect before deciding.
lessons.referenceAnswer: The timed operations differ because only one includes fixture construction; a single run may also reflect scheduling, GC, or machine load. Construct the same fixture outside both loops, then b.ResetTimer(), and perform one serialize operation per iteration while keeping the result observable when necessary. Run go test -bench=Serialize -benchmem -count=10 for each comparable implementation under the same toolchain and machine conditions; compare distributions of ns/op and allocs/op or B/op. If setup or cache behavior is part of production use, benchmark that separately and label it.
selfCheckCriteria: Identifies unequal timed work and single-run noise rather than asserting a 20% win.
Places equivalent setup outside both timed loops and retains the result when needed.
Compares repeated timings and allocation metrics under the same environment.
lessons.provenance: Go 1.22+; reviewed against Go testing package benchmark API (pkg.go.dev/testing#hdr-Benchmarks), go test flags (pkg.go.dev/cmd/go#hdr-Testing_flags); benchstat (pkg.go.dev/golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Diagnose a blocked goroutine and make a result send safe when its receiver abandons the work.
lessons.title: Find a goroutine blocked on a send
lessons.explanation: A goroutine that blocks on a channel send after its receiver returns can stay alive indefinitely. A context does not interrupt an unconditional send: the goroutine must select on ctx.Done() at that boundary. Use a goroutine profile or a bounded test that repeatedly cancels requests to find persistent blocked stacks; a single runtime.NumGoroutine value is noisy and not proof by itself. Avoid closing a results channel from a receiver merely to unblock a sender, since sending to a closed channel panics. Assume Go 1.22 and standard context and runtime/pprof behavior.
lessons.workedExample: A search worker computes a result and executes results <- value on an unbuffered channel, but the handler returned after a timeout. The goroutine profile shows it waiting in a channel send. Changing the send to select { case results <- value: case <-ctx.Done(): return } lets it exit when the handler cancels its derived context. Downstream blocking calls must also receive ctx; the select alone cannot interrupt an earlier non-cancellable call.
lessons.exercise: Given func worker(ctx context.Context, out chan<- int) { n := slow(ctx); out <- n }, write a cancellation-aware send and show how the caller cancels on exit. Explain how you would check for persistent leaks without asserting an exact global goroutine count.
lessons.referenceAnswer: func worker(ctx context.Context, out chan<- int) { n := slow(ctx); select { case out <- n: return; case <-ctx.Done(): return } }. The caller uses ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent); defer cancel(); go worker(ctx, results) and passes the same ctx into slow if it supports cancellation. A test can cancel many requests, wait within a bounded deadline for workers to signal exit via a WaitGroup, and inspect goroutine profiles if workers remain; do not depend on one exact runtime.NumGoroutine() value.
selfCheckCriteria: Selects between the send and ctx.Done() instead of closing the channel from the receiver.
Shows caller-owned cancellation and propagation into slow work.
Uses a bounded worker-exit test or profile, not a brittle exact global count.
lessons.provenance: Go 1.22+; reviewed against Go context package (pkg.go.dev/context), runtime/pprof goroutine profiles (pkg.go.dev/runtime/pprof), Go blog Pipelines and cancellation (go.dev/blog/pipelines); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Choose the channel-close owner so consumers can range safely without racing a send.
lessons.title: Close a channel only when producers are done
lessons.explanation: Closing a Go channel signals that no more values will be sent; it is not a broadcast command to stop arbitrary senders. A send on a closed channel panics, and closing a closed channel also panics. The sending side must coordinate completion before close, often via a WaitGroup when there are multiple producers. A receiving side should not close a channel it does not own. Cancellation can be signalled separately with a context, while channel closure means end of values. Assume Go 1.22 standard channels and sync.WaitGroup.
lessons.workedExample: Three producers write jobs to one output channel. A coordinator starts them with wg.Add(3), each defers wg.Done(), and a separate goroutine calls wg.Wait(); close(out). The consumer uses for job := range out; the range finishes only after all sends and the close. If the consumer stops early, producers need a selectable cancellation path too; simply closing out from the consumer would race active sends.
lessons.exercise: A consumer wants to stop reading an unbuffered stream while two producers may still send. Who may close the stream, when should that happen, and how can the consumer ask producers to stop? Explain what happens if the consumer closes the stream immediately.
lessons.referenceAnswer: The producer coordinator closes the stream after both producers return, e.g. via wg.Wait(); close(stream) in a coordinator goroutine. The consumer cancels a shared context; each producer selects on ctx.Done() while sending, exits, and signals Done. The consumer must not close stream while producers may send: a later send would panic. Cancellation and closure have different meanings; close is the final end-of-stream signal, not the request to stop producers.
selfCheckCriteria: Identifies the sending coordinator as closer after all producers have exited.
Uses context cancellation to request early stop and accounts for blocked sends.
Explains the panic risk of consumer-initiated close while senders run.
lessons.provenance: Go 1.22+; reviewed against Go language specification Close and Send statements (go.dev/ref/spec#Close; go.dev/ref/spec#Send_statements), Go blog Pipelines and cancellation (go.dev/blog/pipelines), sync.WaitGroup (pkg.go.dev/sync#WaitGroup); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Add operation context to a Go error without losing errors.Is matching or inventing success.
lessons.title: Wrap errors while preserving their identity
lessons.explanation: In Go 1.22+, fmt.Errorf with %w wraps an error so callers can inspect its identity with errors.Is or errors.As. %v formats an error as text but does not preserve its chain. Add a useful operation and input identifier without leaking credentials or sensitive payloads. Return nil only when work succeeded; do not replace a concrete failure with a generic string. errors.Is compares against sentinel errors, including those wrapped through several layers. An error can be handled at one layer or propagated, but avoid logging and returning the same failure repeatedly.
lessons.workedExample: A read helper gets os.ErrNotExist from a file open. Returning fmt.Errorf("read configuration: %w", err) lets the caller use errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) to offer a missing-file message. Returning fmt.Errorf("read configuration: %v", err) prints the same words but loses that matching relationship. Do not include file contents or tokens in the wrapping message.
lessons.exercise: Implement loadSettings(path string) ([]byte, error) using os.ReadFile. Return data on success; on failure add operation context so the caller can still match os.ErrNotExist. Show the caller check, and say what you would avoid including in the error message.
lessons.referenceAnswer: func loadSettings(path string) ([]byte, error) { data, err := os.ReadFile(path); if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("load settings: %w", err) }; return data, nil }. The caller uses if errors.Is(err, os.ErrNotExist) { /* offer setup guidance */ }. Import errors, fmt, and os as needed. Avoid embedding the contents, secrets, or untrusted payloads in the error; an appropriate non-sensitive path can be logged at a controlled boundary if policy permits.
selfCheckCriteria: Uses %w to retain the underlying error and tests with errors.Is.
Returns data and nil only on successful os.ReadFile.
Adds operation context without copying secret data into errors.
lessons.provenance: Go 1.22+; reviewed against Go errors package (pkg.go.dev/errors#Is), fmt.Errorf wrapping (pkg.go.dev/fmt#Errorf), os.ReadFile (pkg.go.dev/os#ReadFile); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Design HTTP request deadlines that bound downstream waits while preserving caller cancellation.
lessons.title: Budget HTTP client and server work
lessons.explanation: Go net/http client requests carry a context; canceling it cancels an in-flight request and its response read. An http.Client.Timeout bounds the whole exchange including reading the response body; a Transport has more specific phase limits such as ResponseHeaderTimeout. On the server, r.Context() is canceled when a client connection closes, a request is canceled, or ServeHTTP returns. Derive a shorter deadline from that context for a downstream call and defer cancel; never replace it with Background. A deadline is not a guarantee that non-cooperative external work stops. Assume Go 1.22 net/http and context.
lessons.workedExample: An API handler has an upstream request with a 3-second deadline and a downstream HTTP service that should receive at most 800 ms. It creates child, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 800*time.Millisecond), defers cancel(), and builds the outgoing request with http.NewRequestWithContext(child, http.MethodGet, url, nil). The configured client and transport phase limits also protect connections. On success it closes resp.Body; on deadline error it returns a bounded failure instead of waiting indefinitely.
lessons.exercise: Design a handler that calls a slow downstream HTTP endpoint. State which context to derive from, where to set an 800 ms per-call deadline, when to close the response body, and how an upstream disconnect changes the behavior. Distinguish the deadline from connection and header-phase limits.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Derive child, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 800*time.Millisecond); defer cancel(). Use http.NewRequestWithContext(child, http.MethodGet, target, nil) and client.Do(req), then defer resp.Body.Close() only after Do succeeds and a non-nil response is available. Consume a bounded body before replying. If the client disconnects, r.Context() cancels child early. Configure transport dial/TLS/header phase limits where needed; http.Client.Timeout, if used, caps the entire exchange, not only dial time. Neither timeout forcibly terminates a non-cooperative external side effect.
selfCheckCriteria: Derives from r.Context() and defers cancel, preserving disconnect propagation.
Closes a successful response body and bounds downstream waiting.
Separates whole-exchange and transport-phase limits without claiming remote work stops.
lessons.provenance: Go 1.22+; reviewed against Go net/http Client.Timeout, NewRequestWithContext and Request.Context (pkg.go.dev/net/http#Client; pkg.go.dev/net/http#NewRequestWithContext; pkg.go.dev/net/http#Request.Context), context.WithTimeout (pkg.go.dev/context#WithTimeout); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Close resources you open on normal and exceptional exits without closing caller-owned streams.
lessons.title: Own the stream you open
lessons.explanation: Java try-with-resources closes each AutoCloseable declared in its header when the block exits, including when an exception is thrown. Close happens in reverse declaration order. The exception from the body stays primary; close failures become suppressed exceptions. A method should close resources it creates, but must not silently close a stream supplied by its caller unless ownership was agreed. The example assumes Java 11+ and java.nio.file.Files.
lessons.workedExample: A report method opens a reader with Files.newBufferedReader(path) and a writer with Files.newBufferedWriter(output). It declares both in try (var reader = ...; var writer = ...) { ... }. If copying a line throws, the writer and then reader still close. If writer.close() also fails, inspect the primary exception's getSuppressed() rather than replacing the original read error with a manual finally block.
lessons.exercise: Implement countNonempty(Path path) returning the number of nonblank lines. The method opens its own reader, propagates IOException, and must close the reader on both normal return and failure. Show the resource boundary, not just the counting loop.
lessons.referenceAnswer: long countNonempty(Path path) throws IOException { try (var reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path)) { long count = 0; String line; while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) { if (!line.isBlank()) count++; } return count; } } Import java.nio.file.Files, Path and java.io.IOException. The try header owns the newly opened reader and closes it even when readLine throws; the caller owns the Path, not an open stream.
selfCheckCriteria: Opens the reader inside try-with-resources rather than relying on garbage collection.
Counts nonblank lines and propagates read/close failures without swallowing them.
Does not close a caller-owned stream or Path.
lessons.provenance: Java 21 LTS; original Kontrol starter lesson; reviewed against Oracle try-with-resources (https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/essential/exceptions/tryResourceClose.html), AutoCloseable (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/AutoCloseable.html), Files.newBufferedReader (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/nio/file/Files.html#newBufferedReader(java.nio.file.Path)); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Own the lifetime of a virtual-thread task and propagate cancellation through interruption.
lessons.title: Bound the lifetime of a virtual-thread task
lessons.explanation: Java 21 virtual threads are Thread instances suited to blocking I/O, not a way to make CPU work faster. Thread.startVirtualThread starts work immediately and returns a handle; virtual threads are not pooled. The caller must retain a handle or use an executor, wait for completion at a defined boundary, and decide what to do on timeout or cancellation. Interrupt is a cooperative request: blocking interruptible operations may throw InterruptedException, but application code must not swallow it and continue as if work completed. Bound concurrency to a scarce downstream service separately (for example with a Semaphore), rather than pooling virtual threads.
lessons.workedExample: A request handler starts a virtual thread to query a remote service and retains its Thread handle. If the request is abandoned, it calls interrupt() and waits for the worker to exit at a bounded shutdown boundary. The worker catches InterruptedException from an interruptible wait, restores the interrupt flag if it cannot propagate the exception, and exits after closing any resource it opened. A database driver or non-interruptible library may not stop promptly; interrupt is not a kill switch.
lessons.exercise: A batch starts a virtual thread for each file fetch and returns before any fetch finishes. Describe two lifecycle bugs, how to bound calls to a service allowing only ten simultaneous requests, and what must happen if a waiting caller is interrupted.
lessons.referenceAnswer: The batch needs to retain task handles or submit to a try-with-resources ExecutorService, collect results and failures, and wait before reporting success. Guard each service call with a ten-permit Semaphore, releasing permits in finally; do not use a ten-thread pool to limit virtual threads. If interrupted while acquiring a permit or waiting for completion, propagate InterruptedException or restore the flag and abort the batch, cancel outstanding tasks, and avoid claiming success. Executor close waits for tasks; use an explicit cancellation policy if a bounded exit is required.
selfCheckCriteria: Explains who waits for and cancels tasks rather than abandoning them.
Uses a semaphore to limit scarce I/O rather than pooling virtual threads.
Treats interrupt as cooperative and does not report unfinished work as successful.
lessons.provenance: Java 21 LTS; reviewed Oracle JDK 21 Thread.startVirtualThread and virtual threads guide (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Thread.html#startVirtualThread(java.lang.Runnable); https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/core/virtual-threads.html); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Explain how equality, hash codes, and mutation affect HashMap lookup correctness.
lessons.title: Choose a stable HashMap key
lessons.explanation: HashMap uses hashCode to find a bucket and equals to identify a matching key. Equal keys must have equal hash codes; unequal keys may collide, which affects cost but not correctness. A key whose equality-relevant fields change after insertion may become unreachable by lookup, even with the same object reference. HashMap permits one null key, is not synchronized, and makes no iteration-order promise. Java 21 records make convenient immutable key shapes when their component values are themselves stable; an array component still uses array identity equality unless explicitly handled.
lessons.workedExample: For record CustomerKey(String tenant, long id) {}, two instances with the same tenant and id compare equal and have equal hashes. A map.put(new CustomerKey("a", 17), "paid") can be retrieved with a fresh equal CustomerKey. A mutable key whose tenant changes from "a" to "b" after put can no longer be reliably found in its original bucket. A hash collision between distinct customers does not mean one overwrites the other.
lessons.exercise: A teammate proposes using a mutable List<String> of tags as a HashMap key, then appending a tag after inserting it. Predict the lookup risk. Should a collision imply two values become one? Suggest a safer key, and say whether HashMap is appropriate for concurrent writes.
lessons.referenceAnswer: List equality and hashCode depend on contents; appending changes the hash after insertion, so a later get with that list can miss. Distinct keys with the same hash are separated using equals, not automatically merged. Copy the tags into an unmodifiable snapshot such as List.copyOf(tags) before using it as the key (provided its elements have stable equality), or use a record of stable identifiers. HashMap is not safe for unsynchronized concurrent structural updates; choose suitable synchronization or ConcurrentHashMap with its different null policy.
selfCheckCriteria: Relates equal keys to equal hash codes and explains mutation after insertion.
Does not mistake a hash collision for equality or promise iteration order.
Proposes a stable copied key and addresses concurrent mutation separately.
lessons.provenance: Java 21 LTS; reviewed Oracle JDK 21 HashMap, Object.equals/hashCode, List.copyOf and ConcurrentHashMap (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/HashMap.html; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Object.html#hashCode()); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Write independent parameterized cases for normal, boundary, and invalid inputs.
lessons.title: Parameterize boundary tests in JUnit
lessons.explanation: JUnit Jupiter 5.10 parameterized tests need the junit-jupiter-params artifact in addition to the Jupiter API and engine. @ParameterizedTest invokes the test once per argument row. @CsvSource is useful for simple scalar cases; use @MethodSource when inputs or expected errors need richer types. Give rows meaningful names or a display-name template and assert the specific result. Separate invalid-input assertions from successful-output rows rather than claiming every exception proves the same behavior. Avoid shared mutable test data between invocations.
lessons.workedExample: For a clamp(int n, int lo, int hi) contract with lo <= hi, rows (-2,0,10,0), (0,0,10,0), (6,0,10,6), (10,0,10,10), and (12,0,10,10) exercise below, lower, inside, upper, and above. A separate assertThrows test covers lo > hi only if the production contract specifies an exception.
lessons.exercise: Write a JUnit Jupiter parameterized test for those five clamp cases using @CsvSource. State a second test for inverted bounds if the contract says IllegalArgumentException. Include assertions with expected and actual values; do not assume an undocumented inverted-bounds policy.
lessons.referenceAnswer: @ParameterizedTest(name = "clamp({0}, {1}, {2}) = {3}") @CsvSource({"-2,0,10,0", "0,0,10,0", "6,0,10,6", "10,0,10,10", "12,0,10,10"}) void clampCases(int n, int lo, int hi, int expected) { assertEquals(expected, clamp(n, lo, hi)); } If the stated API rejects inverted bounds, add @Test void rejectsInvertedBounds() { assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> clamp(3, 10, 0)); }. Import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest, org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource, org.junit.jupiter.api.Test, and static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*; include junit-jupiter-params 5.10 on the test classpath.
selfCheckCriteria: Specifies five distinct expected outputs and a parameterized invocation per row.
Uses JUnit Jupiter params and a separate contract-dependent exception test.
Avoids guessing unsupported behavior or sharing mutable case fixtures.
lessons.provenance: Java 21 LTS; reviewed JUnit 5.10 user guide Parameterized Tests and @CsvSource (https://docs.junit.org/5.10.2/user-guide/#writing-tests-parameterized-tests; https://docs.junit.org/5.10.2/api/org.junit.jupiter.params/org/junit/jupiter/params/provider/CsvSource.html); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Distinguish CPU hot paths from allocation pressure using representative JVM recordings.
lessons.title: Read a JVM profile before tuning
lessons.explanation: Java Flight Recorder (JFR) samples execution and records events; a CPU sample stack suggests where sampled running time occurred, not an exact per-method stopwatch or proof of causality. Allocation events and GC pauses answer different questions. Capture under a representative workload after JVM warmup, record JDK version and workload, then compare before and after under similar conditions. JFR settings affect overhead and sampling coverage. Avoid interpreting a single startup recording as steady-state performance or equating high allocation rate with CPU saturation.
lessons.workedExample: A service has 95th-percentile latency spikes. A Java 21 JFR recording shows many execution samples in JSON encoding while allocation events show large temporary byte arrays and GC pause events cluster near spikes. This suggests inspecting payload size and encoding reuse, but does not prove GC caused all slow requests. Correlate request timings, CPU use, allocation rate, and pause durations; change one thing and record again at comparable load.
lessons.exercise: A developer sees an expensive-looking method near the top of a startup CPU profile and proposes caching its output. Describe the next measurements, how to tell CPU from allocation/GC pressure, and why a hotspot alone is not a guaranteed latency win.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Warm up and record the same production-like request mix and concurrency with JFR, noting the JDK and recording settings. Examine execution sample stacks and CPU saturation for CPU cost; inspect allocation events, heap behavior and GC pause durations for allocation pressure. Compare request latency distributions before and after one controlled change. A sampled stack can include work unrelated to the slow request, and a cache may add synchronization or memory pressure, so test the actual end-to-end effect.
selfCheckCriteria: Separates sampled CPU stacks from allocations and GC pause evidence.
Calls for warmup, comparable workload, and before/after latency measurement.
Does not infer causation or guaranteed speedup from one profile.
lessons.provenance: Java 21 LTS; reviewed Oracle JDK 21 JFR runtime guide and jcmd JFR.start (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/jfapi/flight-recorder-api-programmers-guide.pdf; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/jcmd.html); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Design an immutable Java value type that cannot leak a mutable collection through construction or access.
lessons.title: Defend an immutable value boundary
lessons.explanation: A final field prevents reassignment of a reference, not mutation of the referenced object. A record supplies accessors and value equality, but its default constructor and accessor do not defensively copy mutable components. At a boundary, snapshot incoming mutable collections and reject invalid values; prefer immutable element types too. List.copyOf produces an unmodifiable copy and rejects null elements, but deep immutability requires copying mutable elements separately. Java 21 records are appropriate for a compact value carrier, not for concealing shared mutable state.
lessons.workedExample: A receipt record holds List<String> lineItems. If its constructor stores the caller list directly, the caller can add an item later and silently change the receipt. A compact constructor assigning lineItems = List.copyOf(lineItems) takes a snapshot. Its accessor returns that unmodifiable list; strings are immutable so elements are safe in this example. If the list contained mutable arrays, copying only the list would still expose mutable arrays.
lessons.exercise: Design a public Java 21 record Receipt(String id, List<String> lines) used as a snapshot in an audit log. Show validation and defensive copying in the constructor. Explain how you would test caller mutation, accessor mutation, and a null element, and name a limitation if lines held mutable objects.
lessons.referenceAnswer: public record Receipt(String id, List<String> lines) { public Receipt { if (id == null || id.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("id"); lines = List.copyOf(Objects.requireNonNull(lines)); } } Import java.util.List and java.util.Objects. Build a Receipt from an ArrayList, mutate the original, and assert the record still has the old lines; assertThrows(UnsupportedOperationException.class, () -> receipt.lines().add("x")); assertThrows(NullPointerException.class, () -> new Receipt("r", Arrays.asList("ok", null))). This is shallow: for mutable elements make immutable element snapshots as well.
selfCheckCriteria: Shows a compact constructor with validation and List.copyOf snapshot semantics.
Tests both source and accessor mutation plus null-element rejection.
Distinguishes shallow list immutability from deep immutability.
lessons.provenance: Java 21 LTS; reviewed Oracle JDK 21 record classes and List.copyOf (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Record.html; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/List.html#copyOf(java.util.Collection)); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Shut down an executor and handle an interrupted wait without claiming unfinished work completed.
lessons.title: Shut down an executor without losing tasks
lessons.explanation: In Java 21 ExecutorService.close initiates orderly shutdown and waits for submitted tasks, but an unbounded wait is not suitable for every service stop. shutdown() rejects new work while allowing existing work to finish; awaitTermination(timeout, unit) bounds the wait. If it expires, shutdownNow() attempts to interrupt active work and returns queued work that never began. Tasks may ignore interruption, so neither method guarantees termination. If awaitTermination throws InterruptedException, request cancellation, restore the calling thread interrupt flag, and report that termination is uncertain.
lessons.workedExample: A worker service receives a stop signal with 2 seconds of grace. It calls shutdown(), awaits termination for 2 seconds, then calls shutdownNow() if workers remain; it optionally awaits a second bounded period. It logs the count of queued tasks returned by shutdownNow() for recovery instead of pretending they ran. A task blocked in non-interruptible I/O may still remain alive.
lessons.exercise: Write a Java method stop(ExecutorService pool) that gives tasks two seconds to finish, interrupts remaining tasks, then waits one second. On InterruptedException, request immediate shutdown and restore the interrupt flag. Do not print success unconditionally; return whether termination was observed.
lessons.referenceAnswer: boolean stop(ExecutorService pool) { pool.shutdown(); try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) { pool.shutdownNow(); return pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } return true; } catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); return false; } } Import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService and TimeUnit. Production code should record or reschedule the not-started Runnables returned by shutdownNow() if losing them is unacceptable. A true result means termination was observed, not that every submitted task succeeded.
selfCheckCriteria: Calls shutdown before a bounded await and shutdownNow after timeout.
On interruption requests cancellation and restores the interrupt flag.
Distinguishes terminated executor from successfully completed tasks and accounts for queued work.
lessons.provenance: Java 21 LTS; reviewed Oracle JDK 21 ExecutorService shutdown/awaitTermination/shutdownNow/close (https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/api/java.base/java/util/concurrent/ExecutorService.html); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Choose a Spring transaction boundary that keeps related database writes atomic without assuming external calls roll back.
lessons.title: Place a Spring transaction at the write boundary
lessons.explanation: Assume Spring Framework 6.1, proxy-based declarative @Transactional, and a single transactional database. A public service method invoked through the Spring proxy can group repository writes; self-invocation within the same object bypasses proxy advice. By default unchecked RuntimeException and Error trigger rollback, while checked exceptions do not unless rollbackFor is configured. Network calls cannot join a local database transaction by annotation alone. Keep the transaction short, persist a durable outbox event in the same database transaction, and send it asynchronously with idempotent consumption rather than holding locks during a slow external request.
lessons.workedExample: A checkout service writes an order and an outbox row in one @Transactional public method invoked by a controller through the Spring bean proxy. If the order write fails with a runtime exception, neither row commits. A separate dispatcher reads committed outbox rows and calls the email provider; retries can deliver twice, so the receiver or delivery adapter deduplicates by message ID. Putting @Transactional on a private helper called by this service would not create a new proxy boundary.
lessons.exercise: Design an order creation service that saves an order and requests a confirmation email. Specify the transaction entry point, what goes in the local transaction, failure/retry behavior for email, and the behavior if a checked IOException escapes. State why calling a second annotated method on this within the same bean is unsafe as a boundary.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Expose a public @Transactional service method through a Spring bean proxy; write order and outbox message atomically in one database transaction and return after commit. An outbox worker retries email with a stable message ID; never claim the DB can roll back an email already sent. If a checked IOException must roll back this transaction, declare @Transactional(rollbackFor = IOException.class) or translate it to an appropriate unchecked failure; by default checked exceptions do not trigger rollback. A call to this.annotatedMethod() bypasses the proxy in proxy mode; move the boundary to an externally invoked bean or use a suitable programmatic transaction.
selfCheckCriteria: Locates the proxy-invoked service transaction around both local writes, not the network call.
Handles default checked-exception rollback policy and self-invocation correctly.
Includes durable outbox and duplicate-safe retry rather than promising exactly-once email.
lessons.provenance: Java 21 LTS; reviewed Spring Framework 6.1 transaction declarative semantics and rollback rules (https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/6.1/data-access/transaction/declarative/annotations.html; https://docs.spring.io/spring-framework/reference/6.1/data-access/transaction/declarative/rolling-back.html); docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Make retries of the same payment safe using a durable account-scoped idempotency key.
lessons.title: Make a retried payment safe
lessons.explanation: A network timeout does not tell a client whether a write committed. An idempotency key lets the client retry the same logical operation without creating a second one. Scope the key to the authenticated account, record a canonical request fingerprint and outcome durably, and reject reuse with different input. The key claim and the business write need one atomic boundary; a process-local cache or read-then-insert leaves a race. Define retention and what happens after expiry rather than promising exactly-once delivery across all systems.
lessons.workedExample: Account A sends POST /payments with key K and amount 25. The server atomically reserves (A,K) with a unique constraint and associates the payment and recorded result. The response is lost. A retry of the same payload and key returns the recorded result, including the payment ID, without charging again. Account B can independently use K. If A retries K with amount 30, the server returns a conflict instead of silently replaying the 25-unit result.
lessons.exercise: Sketch a create-payment endpoint where two identical requests with the same account and key arrive concurrently, then one client times out. Specify the uniqueness boundary, how the loser obtains a result, what a different payload does, and what you would do if the external payment provider cannot participate in your database transaction.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Require a client-generated key and store (accountID, key) under a unique index with a canonical payload digest. In a database transaction, claim that pair and create one local payment intent/result; the competing request waits for the winner or reads the committed result. On a different digest return conflict. Pass a stable derived key to a provider that supports idempotency and reconcile uncertain provider outcomes; do not claim the local transaction makes an external charge atomic. Document key lifetime and retry behavior after expiration.
selfCheckCriteria: Uses a unique account-scoped key and compares the request fingerprint.
Handles simultaneous claims atomically and replays the same committed result after a lost response.
Acknowledges external side-effect uncertainty and defines a provider/reconciliation strategy and retention limit.
lessons.provenance: Original Kontrol starter lesson; reviewed against Stripe idempotent requests (https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests) and AWS prescriptive guidance idempotency pattern; docs/learning-curriculum.md; not a provider-specific guarantee

lessons.objective: Choose a rate-limit enforcement boundary and explain its consistency and failure behavior.
lessons.title: Limit requests across API replicas
lessons.explanation: A per-process counter cannot enforce a shared quota when requests land on different replicas. Define the principal and operation being limited, the window or token refill rule, and the desired bound before choosing a store. A shared atomic token-bucket operation can give a per-key bound while its store is reachable; replicated or eventually consistent counters permit overshoot. Rate limiting is not authorization: authenticate before deriving the key, bound unauthenticated traffic separately, and do not trust a caller-supplied tenant ID. Specify how store outages affect availability and abuse risk.
lessons.workedExample: A login API permits an initial burst of five attempts per account across three replicas, then refills one token every 12 seconds (average five per minute). This does not enforce a strict maximum of five attempts in any rolling minute: refilled tokens can be spent in that minute too. Each replica atomically consumes from the same capacity-five bucket keyed by normalized account identifier. Separate local capacity-five buckets could permit a burst of fifteen attempts across the replicas. The API returns 429 with a bounded retry hint when depleted; a separate IP-level guard limits unknown accounts without assuming IP identifies one user.
lessons.exercise: Design a 100-requests-per-minute limit for authenticated tenant writes served by six replicas. Identify the key, atomic operation, consistency guarantee, 429 response, observability, and policy if the counter store fails. Discuss a local fallback versus rejecting writes.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Derive tenant ID from the verified principal and key an atomic shared token bucket by tenant and write class. Set capacity 100 and a refill rate matching the published policy (a token bucket permits bursts, unlike a strict rolling window); consume before accepting work and return 429 plus a conservative Retry-After when empty. Track allowed, rejected, store-error and per-tenant aggregate saturation without logging secrets. If the store is unavailable, a local bounded fallback favors availability but can exceed the global limit by up to the number of replicas; fail-closed for costly or abuse-sensitive writes if that is unacceptable. Neither option is globally exact during partition; document the policy.
selfCheckCriteria: Keys by verified tenant and uses one atomic cross-replica decision rather than local counters.
States bucket burst behavior and a bounded rejection response with observable error paths.
Makes outage tradeoff explicit and does not promise strict global enforcement with a local fallback.
lessons.provenance: Original scenario; reviewed against IETF RFC 6585 section 4 (429) and RFC 9110 Retry-After; docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Design notification delivery with durable retries and explicit duplicate handling.
lessons.title: Deliver notifications despite worker crashes
lessons.explanation: An acknowledgement tells a broker that a delivery attempt finished; it does not prove the external notification was seen exactly once. A worker can send an email and crash before acknowledging, causing redelivery. Persist the notification intent alongside the triggering database change, publish it reliably, and acknowledge only after durable handling. Use a stable notification ID for deduplication where supported, bounded retry with a dead-letter path, and a delivery status that distinguishes queued, attempted, and provider-accepted from user-read. An outbox prevents lost intents but does not make a remote provider transactional.
lessons.workedExample: An order commit writes an order and outbox event N42 in one transaction. A publisher may enqueue N42 twice after a crash; the worker records N42's provider request key and submits it. If it crashes after provider acceptance but before acknowledgement, a retry uses the same provider idempotency key or reconciles status before sending again. If the provider lacks deduplication, duplicate emails remain possible and the product must tolerate them.
lessons.exercise: Sketch order-confirmation notification delivery through a queue. An order is committed, the broker briefly goes offline, and later a worker dies after a provider call. Explain durable intent, acknowledgement point, retries, duplicate policy, and what the dashboard may honestly call delivered.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Write the order and an outbox row with stable notification ID in the same local transaction. A retrying publisher transfers the row to the broker and marks publication only after confirmation; publication itself may repeat. The worker sends with the stable ID where the provider supports dedupe, persists attempt/provider status, then acknowledges; after a crash it retries or reconciles uncertain outcomes. Back off transient errors, cap attempts, alert on dead-lettered messages, and provide a manual replay path. Report provider-accepted, not user-read or exactly-once delivery. Without provider idempotency, state that duplicates can still occur.
selfCheckCriteria: Prevents an order commit without a durable notification intent during broker outage.
Addresses crash-after-send redelivery with stable identity and an honest duplicate policy.
Separates broker acknowledgement and provider acceptance from actual receipt or reading.
lessons.provenance: Original scenario; reviewed against AWS SQS at-least-once delivery and AWS prescriptive guidance transactional outbox pattern; docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Bound retries by deadline and capacity rather than amplifying an overloaded dependency.
lessons.title: Spend a retry budget wisely
lessons.explanation: Retries can turn one user request into many backend calls exactly when the backend is struggling. Retry only failures classified as transient and only operations safe to repeat, or use an idempotency key for writes. Put one retry layer near the call boundary, cap total attempts and elapsed time under the caller deadline, and use exponential backoff with jitter to avoid synchronized bursts. A Retry-After hint can inform a delay but cannot override the remaining deadline. Track original requests, attempts, and successes separately; a retry budget limits extra load, not just per-request latency.
lessons.workedExample: A service has a 900 ms remaining deadline and a read dependency returns 503 after 100 ms. It can schedule at most one jittered retry after 150–250 ms with a 300 ms per-attempt timeout, leaving time to respond. If the first attempt takes 700 ms, there is insufficient budget and the service fails promptly. Three nested layers each attempting three times could instead issue up to 27 dependency requests for one caller.
lessons.exercise: A checkout write times out after 700 ms of a 1-second deadline. The gateway and two internal services each retry three times, and the provider's result is uncertain. Should the gateway retry immediately? Give a safe decision rule, maximum amplification of this policy, and metrics to determine whether a new policy helps.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Do not blindly retry an uncertain non-idempotent charge with only 300 ms left. Return an uncertain/pending result for reconciliation, or retry only with a stable provider-supported idempotency key and enough deadline for a bounded attempt. Three attempts at each of three layers can multiply to 27 leaf calls per original request; consolidate retries at one layer, cap attempts and extra calls with a shared retry budget, and add exponential jitter for genuinely transient errors. Measure attempts per original request, dependency load, final success and p95/p99 latency, timeouts and duplicate charges. A 4xx validation failure is not a transient retry candidate.
selfCheckCriteria: Rejects blind retry of an uncertain charge and uses stable idempotency or reconciliation.
Computes 27 possible leaf calls and limits attempts by remaining deadline and shared budget.
Distinguishes transient from permanent failures and measures amplification as well as success.
lessons.provenance: Original scenario; reviewed against AWS Builders' Library Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter and RFC 9110 retry semantics; docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Explain the stale-read window and invalidation race in a cache-aside design.
lessons.title: Know when a cached value is stale
lessons.explanation: In cache-aside reads, a miss loads from the source and populates the cache; writes update the source and invalidate the corresponding key after commit. A TTL limits how long an unrefreshed entry survives, not the maximum staleness under every race. A concurrent reader can miss, fetch the old value before a write commits, then populate the cache after the writer invalidates it. Define freshness needs per data class; versioned keys or version checks can avoid stale fills, while strongly consistent reads may bypass the cache. Cache availability and origin load also matter during eviction storms.
lessons.workedExample: A product price cache has a 60-second TTL. Reader R misses and reads price 20 from the database. Writer W commits price 25 and deletes the cache entry. R then fills the cache with 20. Buyers could observe 20 until that entry expires unless a version guard rejects R's old fill or the checkout path reads authoritative pricing. Simply invalidating after commit did not serialize R's read with W's write.
lessons.exercise: A catalog page tolerates 60 seconds of stale price display, but checkout must charge the current authoritative price. Explain a cache-aside read and post-commit invalidation, the miss/fill race, and a separate strategy for checkout. What signals would reveal a stale-data or stampede problem?
lessons.referenceAnswer: Use cache-aside with a 60-second TTL for browsing: on miss load source and fill, and after a committed price update evict its key. A pre-commit read can fill an old value after eviction; if this exceeds the browsing contract, compare source versions when filling or use versioned cache keys. Checkout revalidates price against the authoritative store under its transaction/consistency policy rather than trusting the display cache. Track cache hit and miss rates, origin traffic, version mismatches and observed age; single-flight or bounded refresh can reduce concurrent miss storms. TTL alone is not a consistency guarantee.
selfCheckCriteria: Explains the stale fill after invalidation instead of promising instant consistency.
Separates tolerant browsing reads from authoritative checkout decisions.
Specifies a freshness bound or version guard and monitors origin pressure on misses.
lessons.provenance: Original scenario; reviewed against AWS Builders' Library Caching challenges and strategies and Redis cache-aside documentation; docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Apply backpressure with bounded queues and explicit overload responses.
lessons.title: Keep a busy worker queue bounded
lessons.explanation: A queue decouples arrivals from workers, but an unbounded backlog converts a throughput shortfall into growing wait time and memory use. If input averages more than sustainable service rate, no finite queue can absorb it indefinitely. Set a maximum in-flight and waiting count, measure queue age as well as depth, and decide whether producers wait, shed low-priority work, or receive an overload response. Limit retry traffic too: rejecting work without a client backoff contract can worsen overload. Durable queues protect accepted work; they do not manufacture processing capacity.
lessons.workedExample: Four workers each complete 25 image jobs per second, while 150 jobs per second arrive for a minute. The 50-job-per-second deficit adds roughly 3,000 jobs if arrivals continue. With a queue cap of 500, the system reaches capacity in about 10 seconds from empty, then rejects or delays new submissions. A 202 response means a job was durably admitted, not processed; a full queue should not return 202 for work it discarded.
lessons.exercise: Design an image-processing intake with four 25-job/s workers, 150-job/s burst arrivals, and a 500-job queue. Estimate when the queue fills from empty and choose admission, client response, retry guidance, and two overload metrics. How would you preserve already accepted jobs on restart?
lessons.referenceAnswer: Capacity is 100 jobs/s, leaving 50 jobs/s excess; 500 waiting slots fill in about 10 seconds absent other effects. Persist accepted jobs before returning 202 and ensure workers acknowledge after durable completion; during saturation return 429 or 503 with bounded backoff guidance rather than silently drop work. Apply per-client admission limits and jittered client retry to avoid a synchronized surge. Observe oldest-job age, depth, rejection rate and completion throughput; reduce admission or add capacity when sustained demand exceeds service rate. On restart recover durable unacknowledged jobs, accepting possible duplicate processing and using stable job IDs to deduplicate effects.
selfCheckCriteria: Computes the 50-job/s deficit and approximate 10-second fill time.
Never calls rejected or merely queued work completed; defines an overload response.
Uses durable admission and bounded retry plus queue-age and throughput signals.
lessons.provenance: Original scenario; reviewed against AWS Builders' Library Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs and RFC 6585 section 4; docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Choose a partition key that distributes writes without breaking the main read path.
lessons.title: Partition an event store without hotspots
lessons.explanation: A partition key determines where records are written and which queries can target a bounded set of partitions. A timestamp-only key can hotspot the current interval, while random distribution makes a per-tenant timeline expensive to read. Start with query and write rates, distribution and growth, then choose a composite or bucketed key. A very large tenant may still create a hot partition; split it into deterministic buckets and merge bounded results when reading. Cross-partition ordering and transactions require an explicit contract rather than assuming one global sequence.
lessons.workedExample: An audit service writes events for 10,000 tenants; most need a recent tenant timeline, but one tenant generates half of all writes. Keying only by day concentrates today's traffic, while hash(tenantID) makes tenant reads local but leaves the large tenant hot. Bucket that tenant by a stable hash of event ID into, say, 16 lanes within a time interval; read its 16 lanes for a recent window and merge by event timestamp plus ID as tie-breaker. The lane count and read fan-out need measurement.
lessons.exercise: Design partitioning for a multi-tenant audit log with per-tenant last-24-hour queries, append-only writes and one tenant producing 50% of traffic. Specify a key, how to route that hot tenant, bounded timeline reads, ordering limits and a migration signal when the distribution shifts.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Partition by tenant and coarse time bucket for normal tenants so recent reads target a few bounded ranges; measure per-partition write rate and storage. For the exceptional tenant, add deterministic lanes using hash(eventID) mod N within each time bucket; route writes by stable ID and query the N lanes for the requested period, merge/paginate by (timestamp, eventID). This spreads writes at the cost of read fan-out and no single-partition total order; use an assigned sequence or explicit ordering policy if stronger order is required. Watch hottest-partition throttles, skew, query fan-out and tenant growth before changing N; plan a versioned routing transition so old and new buckets remain readable.
selfCheckCriteria: Aligns normal partitioning with tenant/time queries and addresses the 50% hot tenant.
Explains lane read fan-out, bounded pagination and lack of automatic global ordering.
Includes skew measurements and a way to read data across a key migration.
lessons.provenance: Original scenario; reviewed against Amazon DynamoDB partition-key best practices and Google Cloud Bigtable schema design guidance; docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Build a recovery plan with tested restore, explicit RPO and RTO, and safe replay.
lessons.title: Recover after a region failure
lessons.explanation: Recovery point objective (RPO) bounds acceptable data loss; recovery time objective (RTO) bounds time to restore service. A backup is not a recovery plan until a restore and application replay have been tested. Asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged writes on failover; a stale secondary must not accept conflicting writes alongside the former primary. Plan detection, fencing or lease ownership, restore validation, and controlled traffic switching. Retained logs and backups need independent protection from operator error or corruption. Replaying jobs can duplicate external effects, so use stable operation IDs and reconcile uncertain outcomes.
lessons.workedExample: An orders service promises RPO 5 minutes and RTO 1 hour. Nightly snapshots alone miss the RPO; periodic snapshots plus tested continuous log archiving could meet it if log gaps are monitored. During a primary-region loss, operators fence the old writer, restore or promote a verified replica, replay logs to a known point, then enable writes and switch traffic. They reconcile payments whose provider acknowledgement was lost rather than blindly resending charges.
lessons.exercise: A service has nightly snapshots, asynchronous replication, a payment provider, and an advertised 5-minute RPO / 60-minute RTO. A region stops responding while the replica is 8 minutes behind. Can the team claim its objectives were met? Outline an ordered recovery and a drill that tests data and duplicate safety.
lessons.referenceAnswer: No: promoting a replica eight minutes behind can lose acknowledged writes beyond the 5-minute RPO; nightly snapshots alone are worse. First declare incident and freeze/fence the old writer to prevent split brain. Determine the latest consistent replica/log point, restore missing archived logs if available and verify order counts/checksums before traffic switch; disclose any remaining loss and measure actual time against 60-minute RTO. Reconcile provider payments by stable operation ID before replaying queued work. Drill with isolated restored infrastructure, timed failover and application-level integrity checks, including replayed jobs, and monitor replication lag and backup restore success between drills.
selfCheckCriteria: Rejects the 8-minute-lag promotion as satisfying a 5-minute RPO without recovered logs.
Fences the old writer and validates a consistent restore before allowing new writes.
Measures RTO in a drill and reconciles uncertain external effects rather than duplicating them.
lessons.provenance: Original scenario; reviewed against AWS Well-Architected Reliability Pillar disaster recovery guidance and Google Cloud disaster recovery planning guide; docs/learning-curriculum.md

lessons.objective: Diagnose an N+1 query pattern and batch related reads while measuring the tradeoffs.
lessons.title: Spot the query hidden in a loop
lessons.explanation: An N+1 read fetches N parent rows with one query, then issues a separate child query for every parent. The number of round trips grows with the result size even when each query is fast. Count database statements for a representative request before optimizing. Fetch children in a bounded batch using parent IDs, then group them in memory; a join or ORM eager-load may also work, but check row multiplication and memory cost. Query count is a diagnostic, not a complete latency measure.
lessons.workedExample: A page shows 20 orders and each customer's display name. One SELECT obtains the orders; a loop calls SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id = ? for each order: up to 21 statements. Collect distinct customer IDs and load their names with one parameterized SELECT ... WHERE id IN (...) (respecting parameter limits); map names by ID and render orders. The result uses two statements for the page, even when a customer appears twice.
lessons.exercise: An endpoint fetches 30 articles in one query, then for each article fetches tags with another query. State the expected query count and outline a two-query rewrite. What should a regression test count, and what must be checked before asserting the rewrite is faster?
lessons.referenceAnswer: The naive path executes 1 + 30 = 31 statements if every article triggers a tag fetch. First fetch the articles, then fetch tags for their IDs in one bounded parameterized batch, grouping returned rows by article ID and using an empty list when no tags exist. An integration test can capture SQL statements for a fixed 30-article fixture and assert the count stays bounded rather than growing per article. Compare representative latency and memory, including large tag fan-out and database parameter limits, before claiming a speedup.
selfCheckCriteria: Counts 31 statements for the stated naive workload.
Batches tag reads and preserves articles with zero tags.
Tests query-count growth and checks fan-out, limits, and measured latency rather than assuming every join is faster.
lessons.provenance: Original Kontrol starter lesson; docs/learning-curriculum.md: Performance / N+1 query diagnosis; database-agnostic example

lessons.objective: Authorize access to each object at the read or mutation boundary, not just at login.
lessons.title: Check the object, not just the login
lessons.explanation: Authentication establishes who is making a request; authorization decides whether that principal can access this particular object. A valid session alone does not authorize an arbitrary ID in a URL. Constrain reads and writes using the server-derived principal and the object's ownership or membership rules. Do not trust an owner ID supplied by the client. Recheck authorization at the mutation boundary, and avoid leaking another user's object details in denied responses.
lessons.workedExample: GET /notes/82 receives an authenticated principal with account ID 7. Note 82 belongs to account 9. A query by note ID alone would disclose it; SELECT ... WHERE id = 82 AND account_id = 7 returns no row. For UPDATE, include both id and account_id in the update predicate and check affected rows, rather than authorizing an earlier read and later updating by id alone.
lessons.exercise: A DELETE /notes/{id} handler checks that the caller is signed in and executes DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = :id. Rewrite the key decision in pseudocode or SQL so account 7 cannot delete account 9's note even by guessing its ID. Explain what the handler returns when no authorized row is found.
lessons.referenceAnswer: Read accountID from the verified server-side session, not request JSON. Execute DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = :id AND account_id = :accountID with bound parameters, inside the write transaction; inspect affected row count. Return a generic not-found response if zero rows changed (assuming the API uses concealment), without confirming whether another account owns the ID. If shared notes exist, replace the ownership predicate with an explicit authorized-membership rule checked in the same write boundary.
selfCheckCriteria: Gets account identity from a verified server-side principal instead of a client field.
Constrains the delete by both object ID and authorized account/membership at mutation time.
Does not expose the existence or content of another account's note on denial.
lessons.provenance: Original Kontrol starter lesson; docs/learning-curriculum.md: Security / Authorization checks; generic SQL pseudocode
